1. Front Med (Lausanne). 2026 Oct 14;13:1980048. doi: 10.3389/fmed.2026.1980048. 
eCollection 2026.

Beyond overall accuracy: subgroup performance and threshold calibration of 
AI-assisted chest radiography for equity-oriented pulmonary tuberculosis 
screening.

Chen W(1), Pan S(1), Zhang Z(1), Shen YY(1), Fan Z(1), Li CE(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Intensive Care Unit, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang 
Chinese Medical University (Zhejiang Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine), 
Hangzhou, China.

Artificial intelligence-assisted computer-aided detection (CAD) can expand 
access to chest radiography interpretation for pulmonary tuberculosis screening 
and triage, but high overall discrimination does not ensure safety at a deployed 
threshold. This focused narrative Mini Review synthesizes evidence on subgroup 
performance, threshold calibration, external validity, and implementation of CAD 
for adult pulmonary tuberculosis. Smear-negative, asymptomatic, and some 
HIV-associated disease may be less radiographically visible, increasing 
false-negative risk. Conversely, previous tuberculosis and competing chronic 
abnormalities reduce specificity and concentrate unnecessary confirmatory 
testing. Sex, age, geography, clinical setting, verification design, and 
software version can further alter operating performance. A numerical threshold 
is therefore not a portable algorithm property but a context-specific clinical 
resource-allocation policy. We propose a lifecycle in which programs define the 
intended use, lock the product and version, conduct representative local 
validation, select an operating point under explicit sensitivity and capacity 
constraints, audit clinically relevant subgroups, and monitor the complete care 
pathway. Stratified thresholds and multivariable models may improve selected 
settings, but current evidence does not justify replacing robust local 
calibration and governance. Prospective evaluations should compare threshold 
strategies under common verification standards and report missed cases, referral 
burden, treatment initiation, and patient-important outcomes.

2. Front Pharmacol. 2026 Oct 14;17:1955011. doi: 10.3389/fphar.2026.1955011. 
eCollection 2026.

Integrating knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation to identify 
clinical pharmacology gaps in infectious disease trial protocols.

Waikar S(1), Ramanathan M(1).

Author information:
(1)Artificial Intelligence and Clinical Pharmacology Laboratory, Department of 
Pharmaceutical Sciences, University at Buffalo, The State University of New 
York, Buffalo, NY, United States.

PURPOSE: Clinical trial protocols contain critical clinical pharmacology 
information that is often scattered across different sections of these lengthy 
documents. The purpose was to evaluate whether a retrieval-augmented generation 
(RAG) protocol review integrated with knowledge graphs (KGs) could be used to 
obtain clinical pharmacology evidence and identify regulatory gaps.
METHODS: Clinical trial protocols were obtained from the Gates Foundation's 
publicly available corpus of clinical trials in low- and middle-income 
countries. The RAG protocol review was used to assess the protocols against Food 
& Drug Administration (FDA) guidance documents for hepatic impairment, 
exposure-response, population PK (PopPK), and physiologically based 
pharmacokinetic modeling (PBPK). Disease-specific KG analyses were conducted for 
tuberculosis (TB), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), malaria, and neglected 
tropical diseases (NTD). KG models connecting studies to drugs, diseases, 
pharmacologic classes, organ-function exclusions, biomarkers, and 
pharmacokinetic (PK) parameter features were obtained.
RESULTS: Across 42 unique trials, the KG contained 223 nodes and 376 edges. TB 
protocols produced the largest disease-specific graph, whereas HIV had the 
highest frequency of PK studies. Gap analysis showed that hepatic impairment 
exclusions in TB were more frequent than PK studies. In the multi-guidance 
evaluation, faithfulness was high, answer relevancy was lower, and the clinical 
pharmacology metric showed guidance-dependent differences.
CONCLUSION: The integrated KG-RAG approach can help highlight potential gaps in 
clinical pharmacology reporting in infectious disease clinical trial protocols.

Surveillance, Detection and Therapeutic Innovation in Antimicrobial Resistance 
in the Age of Polycrisis: From Genomic and Digital Innovation to One Health 
Integration.

Branda F(1), Maria F(2), Alexiev I(3), Demir AB(4), Limon Ö(5), Ceccarelli G(6), 
Scarpa F(7), Russo A(2), Spoto S(8), Ciccozzi M(1).

Author information:
(1)Unit of Medical Statistics and Molecular Epidemiology, Università Campus 
Bio-Medico di Roma, 00128 Rome, Italy.
(2)Infectious and Tropical Diseases Unit, "Renato Dulbecco" Teaching Hospital of 
Catanzaro, 88100 Catanzaro, Italy.
(3)National Reference Confirmatory Laboratory of HIV, National Center of 
Infectious and Parasitic Diseases (NCIPD), 1504 Sofia, Bulgaria.
(4)Department of Medical Biology, Faculty of Medicine, İzmir University of 
Economics, İzmir 35330, Türkiye.
(5)Faculty of Medicine, IUE Medicalpoint Hospital, Yeni Girne Av 1825 S No:12, 
Karşıyaka, İzmir 35575, Türkiye.
(6)Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases, University Hospital 
Policlinico Umberto I, Sapienza University of Rome, 00185 Rome, Italy.
(7)Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Sassari, 07100 Sassari, 
Italy.
(8)Diagnostic and Therapeutic Medicine Department, Fondazione Policlinico 
Universitario Campus Bio-Medico, Via Alvaro del Portillo, 200, 00128 Rome, 
Italy.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by 
interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, 
population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, 
diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial 
intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and 
digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to 
predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current 
implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. 
Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with 
genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem 
levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental 
sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated 
platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial 
AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, 
metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and 
prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including 
bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats 
(CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed 
interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and 
vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One 
Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR 
crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable 
implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

The association between social capital and mental health among older people 
living with HIV: a systematic review.

Xia H(1)(2), Cao X(1)(2), He Y(1)(2), Yang L(1)(2), Yu Q(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Shanxi Provincial Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Clinical 
Decision Support, Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, Shanxi, China.
(2)School of Management, Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, Shanxi, China.

BACKGROUND: Older people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) 
constitute a vulnerable group in society and are at high risk of developing 
mental health problems. Although strengthening social capital is a common 
recommendation to reduce such mental health risks, no systematic review has 
examined the link between social capital and mental health among older people 
living with HIV.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies examining the 
association between social capital and mental health among adults aged ≥50 years 
living with HIV. Seven databases were searched up to November 28, 2025. Studies 
were eligible if they quantitatively assessed at least one dimension of social 
capital in relation to a mental health outcome in this population. Two reviewers 
independently screened studies and assessed risk of bias using the 
Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were 
synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: Among the 9,060 articles identified, 10 articles were included in this 
systematic review. Nine of 10 studies measured social support. Trust and civic 
participation were only partially captured within a broader social capital 
instrument in two reports from the same cohort, and reciprocity and 
bonding/bridging/linking capital were not measured. The instruments used to 
measure both social capital and mental health differed substantially across 
studies, and the dimensions assessed were inconsistently operationalized, which 
limited direct comparability of findings. Among studies measuring social 
support, higher levels were generally associated with lower depressive symptoms 
and better mental well-being, but the strength and significance of associations 
varied. Two reports from the same cohort assessed community/society-level social 
capital, reporting mixed associations. Evidence for outcomes other than 
depressive symptoms was sparse.
CONCLUSION: Overall, research attention to social capital and mental health 
among older people living with HIV remains insufficient. Research in this field 
has overwhelmingly focused on social support, leaving broader dimensions of 
social capital largely unexamined. The available evidence suggests a beneficial 
association between social support and mental health, and heterogeneity in 
measurement instruments and operational definitions further limits comparability 
across studies. Future studies should devote greater attention to social capital 
and mental health in this population by adopting standardized and 
multidimensional social capital measures, and using longitudinal designs to 
clarify directionality.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: The protocol for this systematic review was 
registered in PROSPERO. Unique Identifier: CRD42024537839, 
https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=537839.

Not All Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis Is Equal: Site-Specific Mortality in a 
National Indian Cohort.

Singh UB(1), DiBona K(2), Shaikh S(2), Mattoo SK(3), Rao R(3), Rajan S(3), Kumar 
N(3), Karoly M(2), Chaudhary A(4), Sinha P(2)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Microbiology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New 
Delhi, India.
(2)Boston Medical Center, Boston, MA, United States.
(3)Ministry of Health and Family Welfare Central Tuberculosis Division, New 
Delhi, India.
(4)Wadhwani Institute for Artificial Intelligence, New Delhi, India.
(5)Section of Infectious Diseases, Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian 
School of Medicine, Boston, MA, United States.

Among 777,512 Indian adults with extrapulmonary tuberculosis, in-treatment 
mortality varied over tenfold by site, highest for tuberculous meningitis 
(adjusted odds ratio 12.48 vs. lymph node TB), miliary (5.17), and pericardial 
TB (3.86). Associations of HIV, diabetes, alcohol, and tobacco use with 
mortality varied across sites. Risk-stratified, comorbidity-aware care is 
warranted.

7. HIV Med. 2026 Oct 18. doi: 10.1111/hiv.70323. Online ahead of print.

Pilot study of a ChatGPT-based educational and counselling tool in a specialist 
HIV and sexual health clinic.

Koh MCY(1), Ngiam JN(1), Yong HYJ(2), Puspita T(2), Quah J(2), Mak L(2), Ho 
HW(2), Chia SC(1), Chia T(1), Lye P(1), Wu S(1), Tham SM(1), Salada BMA(1), 
Smitasin N(1), Olszyna DP(1), Archuleta S(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, National University 
Hospital, National University Health System, Singapore, Singapore.
(2)Department of Pharmacy, National University Hospital, National University 
Health System, Singapore, Singapore.
(3)Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore, Singapore, 
Singapore.

OBJECTIVES: Real-world implementation of large language models such as ChatGPT 
to enhance patient education remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility, 
acceptability and attitudes towards a ChatGPT-based counselling tool among 
patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) in a specialist infectious diseases 
clinic.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective clinical implementation study in a 
specialist HIV and sexual health clinic in Singapore from Jan 2025 to December 
2025. Patients interacted with a custom ChatGPT-based chatbot prior to routine 
counselling by physicians or pharmacists. Responses were reviewed with patients 
subsequently during consultation. Post-interaction, patients and HCWs completed 
structured surveys incorporating domains from a validated survey tool: perceived 
risk, anxiety, technology/social influence and intention for future use.
RESULTS: The chatbot was most frequently used for counselling on antiretroviral 
therapy initiation or switching, and sexual health advice. A total of 35 
patients and 35 HCW assessments were analysed. Patients had greater perceived 
risk with the use of the chatbot compared to HCWs, as indicated by lower median 
scores (13, IQR 10-16; vs. 18, IQR 15-21), while anxiety scores were similar. 
Technology/social influence scores were high across both groups (overall median 
20, IQR 19-22). Most participants indicated willingness for future use. 
Qualitative feedback highlighted improved patient understanding and more focused 
consultations, but concerns included lack of contextual nuance and occasional 
inaccuracies.
CONCLUSIONS: The pilot implementation of a ChatGPT-based counselling tool in a 
specialist HIV and sexual health clinic was feasible and generally acceptable to 
patients and HCWs. Further studies are required to evaluate accuracy and 
clinical effectiveness before broader implementation.

8. HIV Med. 2026 Oct 18. doi: 10.1111/hiv.70329. Online ahead of print.

Information quality, understandability, actionability and readability of large 
language models for HIV health education: A cross-platform evaluation.

Hu M(1)(2), Wang Z(3), Zhang J(4), Li X(3), Zhao M(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Public Health and Nursing, Hubei University of Science and 
Technology, Xianning, China.
(2)Department of Cardiology, Huanggang Central Hospital, Huanggang, China.
(3)Health Science Center, Yangtze University, Jingzhou, China.
(4)Zaozhuang Vocational College, Zaozhuang, China.

OBJECTIVES: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate 
health education materials, but their suitability for patient-facing human 
immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We 
assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, 
text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials 
generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education 
questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 
5.4-Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 
3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient 
Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), EQ IP-36, 
DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality 
metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and 
seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with 
Wilcoxon-Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question-level aggregation 
followed by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm comparisons.
RESULTS: Significant family-adjusted differences were observed across platforms 
for all prespecified text-structure, quality/understandability/actionability and 
readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text-structure outcomes, 
PEMAT-P Understandability, PEMAT-P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT-P 
composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after 
family adjustment, whereas EQ IP-36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. 
Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high.
CONCLUSIONS: LLM-generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial 
cross-platform and topic-level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of 
LLMs as expert-reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education 
sources. Direct factual accuracy, guideline concordance, hallucination and 
clinical safety were not assessed.

A report on the 2025 global conference on research and application of Chinese 
herbal medicine-derived extracellular vesicles.

Lu Z(1)(2), Cao Y(1)(2), Shen W(1), Wu Z(1), Li H(1), Li D(3)(4), Chen Z(3)(4), 
Zhao Q(1)(3)(4), Zhao K(3)(4).

Author information:
(1)The Third Clinical Medical College of Guangzhou University of Chinese 
Medicine, Guangzhou 510375, Guangdong, China.
(2)These authors contributed equally to this work.
(3)Guangdong Engineering Research Center of Chinese Herbal Vesicles, Guangzhou 
University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou 510375, Guangdong, China.
(4)Guangzhou Key Laboratory of Chinese Medicine Research on Prevention and 
Treatment of Osteoporosis, The Third Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou University 
of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou 510378, Guangdong, China.

This conference report summarizes the Global Conference on Research and 
Application of Chinese herbal Medicine Derived Extracellular Vesicles-like 
Particles (CHM-EVLPs) held in Guangzhou. The conference gathered worldwide 
scholars to exchange cutting-edge advances in extracellular vesicle (EV) 
extraction, functional modification, disease treatment, and industrial 
transformation via six themed forums covering basic research, fruit EVLPs, 
laboratory testing, HIV intervention, and youth innovation. Experts shared 
standardized separation technologies, engineered modification strategies and 
multi-target therapeutic potentials of plant-derived extracellular vesicles 
(PDVs) against tumors, intestinal disorders, metabolic diseases and 
neurodegenerative injuries, while discussing key bottlenecks including 
large-scale production, quality control and regulatory guidelines. Cross-kingdom 
molecular communication, oral nano-delivery systems and interdisciplinary 
combinations with microneedles and artificial intelligence were highlighted as 
promising research directions. The event promoted international academic 
cooperation, clarified translational challenges of CHM-EVLPs products, and laid 
a foundation for advancing standardized, industrialized and globalized 
development of PDVs to facilitate worldwide medical care improvement.

Bedaquiline pharmacokinetics in drug-resistant tuberculosis: from exposure 
variability to individualized therapy.

Xiong Y(1), Wang JL(2), Wei DY(3)(4), Huang YY(3), Wang MS(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Tuberculosis, Shandong Public Health Clinical Center, Shandong 
University, Jinan, China.
(2)Guangxi Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence for Genetic Diseases of 
Long-Dwelling Nationalities, Baise, China.
(3)Department of Pediatrics, Affiliated Hospital of Youjiang Medical University 
for Nationalities, Baise, Guangxi, China.
(4)Department of Pediatrics, The People's Hospital of Chongzuo, Chongzuo, 
Guangxi, China.
(5)Department of Lab Medicine, Shandong Public Health Clinical Center, Shandong 
University, Jinan, China.

Bedaquiline has transformed the treatment of multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant 
tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) and is now a core component of contemporary all-oral 
regimens. However, translating its distinctive pharmacokinetic properties into 
individualized clinical management remains challenging. Bedaquiline exhibits 
food-enhanced absorption, extensive plasma protein binding, broad but 
heterogeneous tissue distribution, cytochrome P450 3A4-mediated metabolism to 
the N-monodesmethyl metabolite M2, and prolonged persistence caused by tissue 
sequestration and slow redistribution. These features contribute to substantial 
interindividual variability, clinically important drug-drug interactions, 
delayed accumulation, and residual exposure long after treatment 
discontinuation. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the 
absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of bedaquiline; population 
pharmacokinetic models and determinants of exposure variability; target-site 
penetration; pharmacokinetics in children, pregnancy, organ dysfunction, and HIV 
coinfection; and clinically relevant interactions with antituberculosis and 
antiretroviral drugs. We also critically evaluate exposure-efficacy and 
exposure-toxicity relationships, including evidence from bedaquiline-containing 
multidrug regimens, and examine the potential roles of therapeutic drug 
monitoring, minimum inhibitory concentration-normalized exposure indices, and 
model-informed precision dosing. Current evidence supports administration with 
food, avoidance of potent CYP3A inducers, caution during prolonged CYP3A 
inhibition, and intensified electrocardiographic and electrolyte monitoring when 
QT-prolonging agents are combined. Nevertheless, no plasma, M2, 
area-under-the-curve, or susceptibility-normalized exposure target has been 
prospectively validated for routine dose adjustment. Covariate effects 
identified by population models are inconsistent across cohorts, and 
pharmacokinetic evidence remains limited in several special populations. 
Individualized assessment may therefore be appropriate when clinically 
meaningful uncertainty exists, but empirical departure from standard dosing is 
not currently justified. Progress toward precision dosing will require 
standardized sampling and susceptibility testing, measurement of unbound and 
target-site exposure, externally validated pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic 
models, and prospective demonstration that exposure-guided interventions improve 
clinical outcomes.

11. Emerg Microbes Infect. 2026 Dec;15(1):2751675. doi:

Clinical immunogenicity assessment of HIV/AIDS vaccines: current progress and 
future perspectives.

Yu H(1)(2), Wu X(1), Li T(2), Nie J(1).

Author information:
(1)Division of HIV/AIDS and Sex-Transmitted Virus Vaccines, National Institutes 
for Food and Drug Control (NIFDC), State Key Laboratory of Drug Regulatory 
Science, NHC Key Laboratory of Research on Quality and Standardization of 
Biotech Products, NMPA Key Laboratory for Quality Research and Evaluation of 
Biological Products, Beijing, People's Republic of China.
(2)School of Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, Nanjing, People's 
Republic of China.

Developing a safe and effective HIV-1 vaccine remains the cornerstone of global 
efforts to terminate the AIDS pandemic. However, the virus's immense genetic 
diversity and the persistent absence of a universal Correlate of Protection 
(CoP) present formidable barriers. Concomitant with the iterative evolution of 
vaccine design - spanning from protein subunits to mRNA and germline-targeting 
platforms - immunogenicity evaluation frameworks have undergone a critical 
paradigm shift. The field has transitioned from relying on conventional 
serological assays to embracing comprehensive, high-dimensional immune 
profiling. This review delineates the trajectory of milestone clinical trials, 
including RV144, the HVTN series, and the AMP studies, to systematically 
summarize advancements in assessing both humoral and cellular immunity. We 
comprehensively examine core methodologies, such as Binding Antibody Multiplex 
Assays (BAMA), pseudovirus neutralization, Enzyme-Linked Immunospot (ELISpot), 
and Intracellular Cytokine Staining (ICS). Furthermore, we highlight a pivotal 
transition in evaluative logic: moving beyond a singular focus on neutralizing 
antibody titres to integrate Fc-mediated effector functions (e.g. 
Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC) and Phagocytosis (ADCP)) and the 
synergistic roles of polyfunctional T-cells. We also explore the transformative 
potential of burgeoning frontiers, including systems serology, single-cell 
B-cell receptor (BCR) sequencing, and mucosal immunity evaluation. Ultimately, 
we recommend that future evaluation frameworks combine single-cell multi-omics 
technologies with artificial intelligence algorithms and integrate 
multi-dimensional data for analysis, thereby providing a solid theoretical and 
technical foundation for the design of next-generation HIV vaccines.

12. AAPS PharmSciTech. 2026 Oct 15;27(7):328. doi: 10.1208/s12249-026-03560-x.

Polymer-based Vaginal Insert Systems: Engineering Controlled Drug Delivery for 
Women's Health.

Kadam S(1), Dabhoya M(1), Patel R(2), Shah S(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, LJ Institute of Pharmacy, LJK 
University, LJ Campus , Near Sarkhej-Sanand Circle, Off. S.G. Road, Ahmedabad, 
382210, India.
(2)Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, LJ Institute of Pharmacy, LJK 
University, LJ Campus , Near Sarkhej-Sanand Circle, Off. S.G. Road, Ahmedabad, 
382210, India. dr.riya.patel@ljku.edu.in.
(3)Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, LJ Institute of Pharmacy, LJK 
University, LJ Campus , Near Sarkhej-Sanand Circle, Off. S.G. Road, Ahmedabad, 
382210, India. shreeraj.shah@ljinstitutes.edu.in.

Polymer-based vaginal inserts have emerged as a promising approach for localized 
and systemic drug delivery, demonstrating improved therapeutic efficacy, 
prolonged drug residence, controlled release and enhanced patient compliance 
compared to conventional vaginal dosage forms. This article gives a complete 
overview of the design and development of polymer-based vaginal inserts, 
covering the influence of vaginal physiology, mucoadhesion and polymer selection 
on formulation performance. The properties and applications of natural, 
synthetic, and hybrid polymers, and current breakthroughs in fabrication 
technologies such as freeze-drying, solvent casting, hot-melt extrusion, 
electrospinning, and 3D printing are covered. Also examined are several drug 
release techniques such as sustained, swelling-controlled, stimuli-responsive 
and mucoadhesive systems. Moreover, the therapeutic potential of vaginal inserts 
for the treatment of vulvovaginal infections, endometriosis, cervical cancer, 
uterine fibroids, menopause-related illnesses, contraception and HIV prevention 
is emphasized. Finally, the future directions of emerging technologies, such as 
nanotechnology, smart polymers, artificial intelligence, and personalized drug 
delivery systems, are discussed for the clinical translation and enhanced 
efficacy of polymer-based vaginal drug delivery systems for women's reproductive 
health.

Mediating role of sleep in the association between HIV infection and depression: 
a cross-sectional analysis with NHANES data.

Lin Z(1), Ye X(1), Xu K(1), Zhu T(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)College of Artificial Intelligence, Zhejiang A&F University, Hangzhou, 
People's Republic of China.
(2)Shanghai Key Laboratory of Intelligent Information Processing,, Shanghai, 
People's Republic of China.

Depression is a major public health concern and frequently coexists with sleep 
disturbances, particularly among individuals with Human Immunodeficiency Virus 
(HIV) infection. However, it remains unclear to what extent sleep disturbance 
may account for the observed association between HIV infection and depressive 
symptoms. This study examined the associations among HIV infection, sleep 
status, and depressive symptoms and assessed the potential contribution of sleep 
status. Using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 
(NHANES) 2005-2014 cycles, weighted logistic regression, Firth's penalized 
regression, Bayesian mediation analysis, and LightGBM with SHAP interpretation 
were applied. Among 14444 adults, HIV-positive status was associated with higher 
odds of depressive symptoms, but the association was attenuated and became 
non-significant after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, and behavioral 
factors. Sleep quality showed a graded association with depression, with ORs of 
2.17, 5.83, and 13.60 for fair, poor, and very poor sleep. Bayesian mediation 
analysis suggested that sleep disturbance may explain the association between 
HIV infection and depressive symptoms. SHAP analysis identified sleep status as 
the most important predictor of depression. These findings highlight the 
importance of sleep assessment and management for improving mental health among 
individuals with HIV infection.

The 39th International Conference on Antiviral Research (ICAR), hosted by the 
International Society for Antiviral Research (ISAR), took place April 27-May 1, 
2026, at the Cubex Centrum Praha in Prague, Czech Republic. The annual meeting 
brought together scientists from academia, industry, government, and public 
health to present recent advances across antiviral discovery, therapeutic 
development, vaccine research, host-directed approaches, and preparedness for 
emerging and re-emerging viral threats. The 2026 program included plenary and 
award lectures, oral presentations, poster sessions, late-breaking 
presentations, shotgun presentations, and focused scientific sessions spanning 
arboviruses, coronaviruses, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), 
chronic, latent, and persistent viruses, hepatotropic and gastrointestinal 
viruses, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven drug discovery, broad-spectrum 
antiviral drugs, non-respiratory biothreat viruses, and pandemic preparedness. 
The opening plenary featured lectures on influenza virus and hepatitis D virus 
entry inhibition, while ISAR award lectures highlighted major contributions to 
antiviral science, including global virus research, antiviral and vaccine 
development, broad-spectrum antiviral approaches, rational drug design, and 
small-molecule development for yellow fever disease. ICAR 2026 also included 
dedicated activities to support professional development and community building, 
including the Women in Science Roundtable, First Timer and New Member Morning 
Coffee, PechaKucha Competition, the Chu Family Foundation Fellowship 
presentations, ISAR Annual Meeting, and Career Development Interactive 
Roundtable. Overall, ICAR 2026 reinforced ISAR's role as an international forum 
for scientific exchange, interdisciplinary collaboration, and development of the 
next generation of antiviral researchers.

Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted HIV Educational Video for 
Improving HIV Health Literacy Among Indonesian Adolescents.

Wilandika A(1), Yualita P(1), Zahrotunnaqiyah NE(1).

Author information:
(1)Universitas 'Aisyiyah Bandung, Indonesia.

Adolescents in low- and middle-income countries continue to face substantial 
barriers in accessing effective HIV education, despite global efforts in 
prevention. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a culturally adapted HIV 
educational video developed using artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted video 
production tools. The intervention assessed in this study was the educational 
video itself rather than direct interaction with a generative AI system. A 
quasi-experimental design with pre- and posttests and a control group was used 
to evaluate the intervention among 60 high school students. Participants were 
randomly assigned to either a group that received a 10-min AI-generated 
educational video or a control group that received no intervention. The video 
was designed to improve HIV health literacy by addressing four domains: access 
to information, comprehension of core concepts, evaluation of risks, and 
application of knowledge in real-life decisions. Quantitative data were 
collected in May 2024 using a validated scale and analyzed with nonparametric 
tests and analysis of covariance. Students who received the AI-assisted 
educational video demonstrated significantly higher posttest HIV health literacy 
scores than the control group (Mann-Whitney U = 206.5, p < .001). After 
adjustment for baseline scores, analysis of covariance confirmed a significant 
group effect (F(1,57) = 21.70, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.28), indicating a large 
adjusted effect size. The findings highlight the potential of generative AI as 
an innovative, scalable tool for adolescent health education, particularly in 
resource-limited settings. This approach may offer new opportunities for 
integrating digital strategies into school-based health promotion programs.

Analysis of tuberculosis prevalence surveys in Africa: evidence to change the 
status quo in case finding.

Mukherjee JS(1), Ndayizigye M(2), Lee C(3), Gilmore M(4), Benali S(5), Maama 
L(6), Andom AT(7).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Brigham, Boston, MA, United 
States.
(2)Partners In Health, Boston, MA, United States.
(3)Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, London, United 
Kingdom.
(4)Northeastern Bouve College of Health Sciences, Boston, MA, United States.
(5)Ariadne Laboratory, Boston, MA, United States.
(6)Government of Lesotho, Maseru, Lesotho.
(7)Partners In Health, Maseru, Lesotho.

INTRODUCTION: Lesotho has among the world's highest TB prevalences and the 
national program finding only 50% of incident cases. Lesotho underwent its first 
TB prevalence study in 2019 in reviewing this study, the authors recognized that 
the standard measures for screening and diagnosis TB often failed to detect the 
presence of culture positive pulmonary TB. This review seeks to determine if the 
systematic under detection of culture positive TB by standard methods is true 
among prevalence surveys in Africa.
METHODS: We conducted a review to identify TB prevalence surveys conducted in 
Africa from 2011 to 2024. Seventeen surveys meeting inclusion criteria were 
identified. For each survey, we extracted the proportion of culture-confirmed TB 
cases that were also identified by symptom screening, chest X-ray (CXR), sputum 
smear microscopy, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF. We additionally tabulated national HIV 
prevalence, HIV co-infection rates reported by national TB programs, and HIV 
co-infection rates documented in the prevalence surveys themselves.
RESULTS: TB prevalence across the 17 surveyed countries ranged from 119 per 
100,000 population in Rwanda to 737 per 100,000 in South Africa, with Lesotho 
(581), Tanzania (590), Zambia (638), Kenya (558), Nigeria (524), Uganda (401), 
Namibia (465), Malawi (452), Ghana (356), Eswatini (352), Mozambique (334), 
Zimbabwe (344), Gambia (212), Sudan (183), and Ethiopia (183) recording 
intermediate burdens. Symptom screening missed an average of 50% of 
culture-confirmed pulmonary TB cases across all surveys. Smear microscopy missed 
approximately 60% of bacteriologically confirmed cases. GeneXpert, while more 
sensitive, still missed an average of 30-35% of culture-confirmed cases even 
under rigorous study conditions. In contrast, CXR demonstrated concordance 
exceeding 80% with culture-confirmed TB across almost all surveyed countries. 
HIV co-infection among TB patients in prevalence surveys was consistently lower 
than rates reported in national TB programs, suggesting systematic 
underrepresentation of HIV-positive individuals in survey populations.
CONCLUSION: Symptoms-based screening and GeneXpert alone are insufficient to 
detect the majority of people with active, bacteriologically confirmed TB. Chest 
X-ray, with markedly higher sensitivity than symptom screening or molecular 
testing under real-world survey conditions, should be repositioned as a primary 
screening tool in high-burden settings.

PrEP Use and Willingness Cascades Among Transgender Women in 11 Asian Countries: 
Findings From the PrEP APPEAL Cross-Sectional Online Survey.

Wolter A(1)(2), Wirawan GBS(1)(3), Chan C(1), Janamnuaysook R(4)(5)(6)(7), 
Tieosapjaroen W(8)(9), Boonyapisomparn H(10), Cassell MM(11), Zhang

Author information:
(1)Kirby Institute, University of New South Wales (UNSW) Sydney, Sydney, New 
South Wales, Australia.
(2)School of Population Health, UNSW Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.
(3)Center for Public Health Innovation, Faculty of Medicine, Udayana University, 
Denpasar, Indonesia.
(4)Institute of HIV Research and Innovation (IHRI), Bangkok, Thailand.
(5)Amsterdam University Medical Centers (UMC), Department of Global Health, and

(6)Amsterdam Institute for Immunology & Infectious Diseases, Amsterdam, the

(7)Center of Excellence in Transgender Health, Chulalongkorn University,

INTRODUCTION: Transgender women in Asia face a high HIV burden, yet remain 
underrepresented in pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) research. Despite increases 
in PrEP availability, uptake among trans women remains low. This study examines 
PrEP awareness, use, and willingness among trans women across 11 Asian 
countries.
METHODS: Data were drawn from the 2022 PrEP Product Awareness, Preferences, and 
Past Experiences Among Transgender Women and Men Who Have Sex with Men (PrEP 
APPEAL) study, a multi-country cross-sectional online survey. Two PrEP cascades 
were constructed: one assessing use (awareness, lifetime use, current use) and 
the other assessing willingness (risk, interest, and willingness to pay). 
Logistic regression models were used to identify factors associated with 
lifetime PrEP use and willingness to use PrEP.
RESULTS: Of 1178 trans women participants, 80.0% (n = 942) had heard of PrEP. 
Among those who were PrEP-aware, 62.6% (n = 590/942) reported ever using it, and 
of these, 78.1% (n = 461/590) were current users. Among PrEP-naïve participants 
classified as at risk of HIV (n = 265), 60.0% (n = 159/265) were willing to 
initiate PrEP, yet only 34.0% (n = 54/159) were also willing to pay. Lifetime 
PrEP use was positively associated with wider country-level PrEP access 
(aOR = 4.34; 95% CI: 3.03-6.21), genital surgery (aOR = 1.54; 1.03-2.31), 
current romantic relationship (aOR = 1.65; 1.19-2.29), as well as reporting sex 
work (aOR = 1.51; 1.05-2.18), condomless sex (aOR = 1.76; 1.28-2.42), chemsex 
(aOR = 1.98; 1.36-2.87), and a recent sexually transmitted infection diagnosis 
(aOR = 2.28; 1.45-3.59) within the past 6 months. Negative associations included 
older age (aOR per year = 0.94; 0.92-0.96) and discrimination from healthcare 
workers (aOR = 0.66; 0.47-0.93). Willingness to use PrEP was lower among older 
participants (aOR per year = 0.97; 0.94-0.99) and those in countries with wider 
PrEP access (aOR = 0.53; 0.29-0.97), with no significant associations observed 
for behavioural risks.
CONCLUSIONS: PrEP awareness was high among trans women in Asia. PrEP use and 
willingness were influenced by structural barriers (e.g. country-level PrEP 
access), healthcare discrimination, and personal factors (e.g. behavioural 
risks). Scaling up PrEP for trans women requires rights-based approaches and 
commitment to achieve equitable HIV prevention in the region.

Evaluation of a hand hygiene intervention in two primary schools using UV-based 
feedback and AI-assisted image analysis.

Bordas A(1), Colom-Cadena A(2)(3), Aceiton J(2), Martínez-Torres S(1), 
García-Pino A(4), Escaramis G(2), Muntada E(2), Rey-Reñones C(1)(5), 
Gens-Barberà M(1)(6), Casabona J(2)(3)(7), Basora J(1), Martín-Luján F(1)(8).

Author information:
(1)ISAC Research Group (Intervencions Sanitàries i Activitats Comunitàries, 2021 
SGR 00884), Primary Healthcare Research Support Unit-Camp de Tarragona, Jordi 
Gol Primary Care Research Institute (IDIAPJGol), Catalan Institute of Health 
(ICS), Tarragona, Spain.
(2)Centre for Epidemiological Studies of Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV 
in Catalonia (CEEISCAT), Badalona, Spain.
(3)Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP), Badalona, Barcelona, Spain.
(4)Preventive Medicine Department, Joan XXIII University Hospital of Tarragona, 
Catalan Institute of Health (ICS), Tarragona, Spain.
(5)Department of Basic Medical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health 
Sciences, Universitat Rovira i Virgili (URV), Reus, Spain.
(6)Quality and Patient Safety Central Functional Unit, Catalan Institute of

(7)Biomedical Research Centre Network for Epidemiology and Public Health 
(CIBERESP), Carlos III Institute of Health, Madrid, Spain.
(8)Department of Medicine, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Universitat

OBJECTIVES: Hand hygiene prevents infectious diseases in schoolchildren, but 
objective assessment of technique remains largely unexplored in school settings. 
The aim of the present study is to evaluate a school-based intervention on hand 
hygiene in primary schools.
STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a controlled school-based community intervention 
study with school-level allocation, using a before-after repeated-measures 
design in two primary schools in Tarragona, Spain.
METHODS: A total of 126 children aged 8-12 years participated (64 intervention, 
62 control). The intervention combined a 30-min session on the 7-step 
alcohol-based hand rub technique with feedback using fluorescent hand rub and a 
custom UV device. Hand hygiene quality was measured at baseline and at 1, 3, and 
6 months as the proportion of total hand surface area adequately covered, 
including the palmar and dorsal surfaces of both hands. Images were analysed 
using an artificial intelligence-assisted tool to support more standardised 
outcome assessmentLongitudinal effects were analysed exploratorily with a beta 
mixed-effects regression model.
RESULTS: Adjusted hand coverage was similar between groups at baseline. At 1 
month, both schools showed increased adjusted coverage. From 3 months onwards, 
trajectories diverged. The intervention school showed higher adjusted coverage 
than the control school at 3 months (adjusted mean difference 0.031; 95% CI: 
0.010-0.052) and 6 months (0.041; 95% CI: 0.021-0.061).
CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory study suggests that combining structured hand 
hygiene education with immediate UV visual feedback may contribute to sustained 
improvements in hand hygiene technique in primary school settings. The 
AI-assisted image-analysis workflow supported partial standardisation of outcome 
assessment, although the fluorescence-detection step required human supervision.

Towards a justice-based reimagination of digital health research and innovation: 
actionable considerations for learning health systems.

Kalla M(1), Nazarian N(2), Vokey L(3), Van Rensburg C(4), Kewalramani D(5), 
Dlamini S(6), Charani E(6), Ferdous H(7), Celi LA(8), Milanzi C(9), 
Schneider-Kamp A(10).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Digital Transformation of Health, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry 
and Health Sciences, The University of Melbourne, Melbourne, VIC, Australia. 
Electronic address: Mahima.kalla@unimelb.edu.au.
(2)School of Computing and Information Systems, Faculty of Engineering and 
Information Technology, The University of Melbourne, Melbourne, VIC, Australia.
(3)Department of Biology, Mount Saint Vincent University, Halifax, NS, Canada.
(4)Centre for Digital Transformation of Health, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry 
and Health Sciences, The University of Melbourne, Melbourne, VIC, Australia; 
Centre for Health Policy, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Health Sciences, 
The University of Melbourne, Melbourne, VIC, Australia.
(5)Division of Acute Care Surgery, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School,

(6)Division of Infectious Diseases and HIV Medicine, Groote Schuur Hospital, 
University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa.
(7)Centre for Digital Transformation of Health, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry 
and Health Sciences, The University of Melbourne, Melbourne, VIC, Australia.
(8)Laboratory for Computational Physiology, Massachusetts Institute of 
Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA; Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep 
Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA; Department of 
Biostatistics, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA.
(9)Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Blantyre, Malawi.

The need to embed decolonising methodologies in health-care practice has been 
recognised globally. The term decolonising health, which has become a topic of 
increasing public and academic discourse since 2021, refers to the dismantling 
of colonial systems of dominance and oppression ingrained within health systems 
and structures. Despite the growing recognition of the need for decolonisation 
in broader health research and practice, the application of a decolonial lens to 
the rapidly evolving field of digital health remains largely underexplored. An 
active commitment to decolonisation should be driven by a quest for social 
justice. However, a key concern for those committed to decolonisation in any 
field of inquiry is the continuing hegemony of western Eurocentric knowledge and 
knowledge systems that dominate much of the global research machinery. Hence, we 
suggest that decolonisation of digital health should start at the ontological 
level of coloniality. In this Viewpoint, we present a justice-based 
reimagination of digital health using the established research paradigm framing 
of ontology, epistemology, axiology, and methodology. We also map decolonial 
recommendations across the learning health system model and provide a 
translational reflexivity checklist to support digital health project teams in 
decolonising research and innovation activities.

BACKGROUND: Clinically diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis (cPTB, PTB diagnosis 
despite negative bacteriological results) accounts for 36% of global PTB 
notifications, but factors influencing the diagnosis and its relationship with 
mortality are not well-characterized. We aimed to identify factors associated 
with cPTB and assess its association with mortality.
METHODS: Secondary data analysis of a prospective TB diagnostic cohort that 
evaluated the performance of artificial intelligence in detecting TB and 
COVID-19 using digital chest X-rays (dCXRs) among adults in Zambia. Logistic and 
Cox regression analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: Among 582 PTB patients, median age was 36 (IQR: 28-45) years, 70.6% 
were male and 50.3% had cPTB. Previous TB history (aOR 3.31, 95% CI 2.13-5.13), 
age ≥50 (aOR 2.36, 95% CI 1.31-4.21), symptom duration ≥2 weeks (aOR 0.60, 95% 
CI 0.39-0.93) and dCXR interpretation of pneumonia (aOR 0.34, 95%CI 0.18-0.64) 
were associated with cPTB. Compared to bacteriologically confirmed PTB, cPTB was 
not associated with increased mortality hazard (aHR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.25-2.11).
CONCLUSIONS: Half of PTB diagnoses were cPTB despite availability of molecular 
testing. While mortality was not increased among cPTB patients, there is an 
urgent need to improve TB confirmation to enhance diagnostic accuracy and ensure 
appropriate treatment.

    doi: 10.1001/jamacardio.2026.4084.

IMPORTANCE: Heart failure (HF) is a common condition with substantial 
geographical variation in its prevalence and underlying etiologies. Consistent 
and comparable data on the burden of HF within populations are needed to inform 
health system priorities.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate the global burden of HF.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cross-sectional study estimates disease 
burden using Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 
methodologies to integrate multiple information sources. Data come from 204 
countries and territories from 1990 to 2023 representing the global population 
with prevalent HF.
EXPOSURE: HF and underlying etiologies.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Estimates with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) for 
the prevalence and years lived with disability (YLDs) for HF by age, sex, 
location, year, and underlying etiology.
RESULTS: Globally, there were 56.0 million (95% UI, 49.9-62.2 million) estimated 
cases of HF in 2023. The estimated prevalence of HF generally increased with age 
for all locations. While ischemic heart disease and hypertensive heart disease 
were the 2 most common etiologies globally among older adults, there was 
substantial variation in etiological pattern by location and age. Congenital 
heart anomalies and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common etiologies in 
children and young adults, while the proportion of HF due to alcohol use peaked 
in middle adulthood. Location-specific estimates highlighted regions with higher 
burden of HF due to specific etiologies, including RHD (south Asia, east Asia, 
Oceania, southeast Asia, central sub-Saharan Africa, eastern sub-Saharan Africa, 
southern sub-Saharan Africa, and western sub-Saharan Africa), alcohol use 
(eastern Europe, Australasia, the Caribbean, and central Europe), and Chagas 
disease (southern, Andean, tropical, and central Latin America).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Heart failure is a significant global public health 
burden, and the impact is likely to increase as populations age. However, most 
HF etiologies can be prevented by interventions that reduce exposure to 
modifiable risk factors, such as elevated blood pressure, excessive alcohol 
consumption, and tobacco use. Etiology- and location-specific estimates can 
provide necessary information for public health officials to determine how best 
to prioritize interventions to reduce HF disease burden.

BACKGROUND: Long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine (CAB+RPV LA) and 
dolutegravir plus lamivudine (DTG/3TC) are HIV-1 antiretroviral therapy regimens 
with different administration routes and dosing frequencies, allowing for 
greater choice.plus.
METHODS: VOLITION is a phase 3b, multicenter, nonrandomized, parallel-group, 
open-label implementation-effectiveness study (NCT05917509) evaluating viral 
suppression on DTG/3TC for up to 16 weeks, followed by a participant-determined 
optional switch to CAB+RPV LA dosed Q2M or continuation of DTG/3TC through Month 
(M) 11/12. Co-primary endpoints were the time to virologic suppression with 
DTG/3TC and the proportion of participants with HIV RNA < 50 copies/mL per the 
Snapshot algorithm at M11 with CAB+RPV LA. Safety and participant experience 
were also assessed.
RESULTS: One hundred and seventy-one participants initiated DTG/3TC. Median time 
to suppression on DTG/3TC was 4.1 weeks (95% confidence interval: 4.1-4.3), with 
98% (n = 167/171) achieving virologic suppression and similar rates observed 
across baseline viral load and CD4+ cell count categories. At Day of Choice 
(DoC), 85% (n = 129/151) of eligible participants chose to switch to CAB+RPV LA. 
At M11, 113/129 (88%) participants maintained suppression with CAB+RPV LA; 1 
participant had confirmed virologic failure with resistance (integrase strand 
transfer inhibitor and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor). Both 
regimens were well tolerated, with no new safety signals observed. Treatment 
satisfaction improved after DoC and remained high with CAB+RPV LA.
CONCLUSIONS: Providing treatment-naive participants with the option to switch to 
CAB+RPV LA as soon as virologic suppression was achieved on daily oral therapy 
allowed them to choose a treatment to meet their individualized needs while 
maintaining virologic suppression, which is essential for long-term treatment 
success and optimized quality of life.

HIV-associated nephropathy: A decade of clinical outcomes, global disparities 
and emerging promise.

Pathiyil DV(1)(2), Wearne N(3), Price B(4), Post F(5)(6), Collier DA(2)(7).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK.
(2)Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Cambridge, UK.
(3)University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa.
(4)National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS), University of Cape Town, Cape 
Town, South Africa.
(5)Kings College London, London, UK.
(6)Kings College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK.
(7)Department of Pathology, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK.

OBJECTIVE: To review the pathogenesis, epidemiology, clinical presentation, 
management and outcomes of HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN), with emphasis on 
global disparities, genetic susceptibility (APOL1) and emerging therapeutic and 
technological advances.
DESIGN: Narrative literature review synthesizing contemporary evidence from 
clinical cohorts, translational research and guideline-based practice, with 
comparative perspectives from high-resource (UK) and low-resource (sub-Saharan 
Africa) settings.
METHODS: Relevant studies were analysed to evaluate mechanisms of disease, 
epidemiological trends, diagnostic approaches, treatment strategies and 
long-term outcomes. Particular focus was placed on APOL1-associated risk, 
antiretroviral therapy (ART) impact and recent developments including artificial 
intelligence (AI) applications and targeted therapies.
RESULTS: HIVAN arises from direct HIV infection of renal epithelial cells in 
genetically susceptible individuals, particularly those with APOL1 risk 
variants. ART has significantly reduced incidence in high-income settings, 
whereas HIVAN remains prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa due to delayed diagnosis 
and limited healthcare access. Clinically, HIVAN presents with proteinuria and 
progressive kidney dysfunction, requiring biopsy for confirmation. Early ART 
initiation improves renal outcomes, supported by adjunctive therapies such as 
renin-angiotensin system blockade and SGLT2 inhibitors. Emerging therapies 
targeting APOL1 and advances in AI-driven risk prediction and diagnostics show 
promise.
CONCLUSIONS: HIVAN reflects an interplay between viral, genetic and 
socio-economic factors. While ART has transformed outcomes in well-resourced 
settings, significant global disparities persist. Future progress depends on 
improving HIV care access, expanding renal services and advancing precision 
medicine approaches, including APOL1-targeted therapies and AI-enabled risk 
stratification.

Diagnostic accuracy of machine-learning-based image analysis for early detection 
of Kaposi sarcoma in people living with HIV.

Innocent DC(1), Innocent IP(1), Innocent RC(1).

Author information:
(1)Centicini Research Lab, Centicini Team Ltd., Abuja, FCT, Nigeria.

BACKGROUND: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) remains one of the most common HIV-associated 
malignancies in sub-Saharan Africa, where diagnostic delays contribute to 
advanced disease and poor outcomes. Machine-learning (ML)-based image analysis 
has emerged as a potential tool to support early KS detection, particularly in 
resource-limited HIV care settings.
AIM: To critically synthesise evidence on the reported diagnostic performance, 
imaging modalities, methodological considerations and clinical implications of 
ML-based image analysis for early detection of KS in people living with HIV.
METHODS: A narrative review with structured literature synthesis was conducted. 
PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched for 
publications from 2010 to 2026. Eligible studies evaluated machine-learning or 
artificial-intelligence models applied to medical images for Kaposi sarcoma 
detection or closely related methodological applications and reported relevant 
diagnostic or imaging outcomes. Data were extracted on study characteristics, 
imaging modality, ML approach, reference standard, diagnostic performance, 
validation strategy and methodological limitations, and findings were 
synthesised narratively across predefined themes.
RESULTS: The principal KS-specific quantitative study reported a sensitivity of 
89% (95% CI: 85-94%) and specificity of 51% (95% CI: 40-61%). These represent 
study-level estimates and were not pooled because of the limited number and 
substantial heterogeneity of KS-specific studies. Diagnostic performance varied 
according to imaging modality, dataset size and validation approach. Dermoscopic 
and histopathological ML applications generally demonstrated stronger reported 
performance, whereas photographic approaches offered greater potential for 
decentralised HIV care. Important methodological limitations included limited 
external validation, small datasets and under-representation of darker skin 
tones.
CONCLUSION: Current evidence suggests that ML-based image analysis may have 
potential as a decision-support tool for early KS detection, particularly for 
screening, triage and referral support in settings where specialist 
dermatological expertise is limited. However, the available KS-specific evidence 
remains preliminary, with substantial methodological heterogeneity, limited 
external validation and insufficient evidence for pooled estimates of diagnostic 
performance. Prospective, externally validated and equity-focused studies are 
required before routine clinical implementation can be recommended.

Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

OBJECTIVES: Manual screening of titles, abstracts, and full texts for 
large-volume knowledge synthesis requires significant time investment. 
Machine-assisted tools offer solutions for facilitating screening. Most 
applications to date have focused on actively reordering citations or suggesting 
screening decisions for reviewers to prioritize relevant studies or on 
automating exclusions based on narrowly defined eligibility criteria. However, 
few tools extend to full-text screening, and among those that report, a majority 
have largely been developed with little engagement of knowledge users. Knowledge 
user input has the potential to foster the relevance of review outcomes and 
uncover nuances such as broader community participation in research, which is 
often variably defined and applied. We aimed to describe a pragmatic 
machine-assisted screening workflow that extends to full-text screening and 
engages knowledge users throughout.
STUDY DESIGN AND SETTING: We implemented a pragmatic machine-assisted workflow 
for screening in a large-volume scoping review of community participatory 
approaches in infectious disease mathematical modeling. The review considered 
studies on any specified population, modeling any infectious disease, and where 
community participation was reported in at least one modeling step. The workflow 
was codeveloped with community researchers, representing community-based 
organizations, who contributed to defining eligibility criteria and screening. 
First, we screened titles and abstracts using a supervised random forest model. 
We then triaged full texts based on keywords and made final classifications 
(inclusion/exclusion) using ridge-penalized logistic regression. We evaluated 
the machine-learning model performances using held-out test sets and 
bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Of 16,629 studies identified in the search, 9841 unique citations 
underwent title and abstract screening and 2786 citations underwent full-text 
screening. Model-based title and abstract screening achieved sensitivity of 
86.7% (95% CI: 84.1-89.4) and area under the curve (AUC) of 86.4% (95% CI: 
84.4-88.3), reducing screening workload by 48.3%. Model-based full-text 
screening achieved sensitivity of 82.6% (95% CI: 66.7-95.8) and AUC of 83.2% 
(95% CI: 74.5-91.9), reducing workload by 81.3%.
CONCLUSION: A machine-assisted screening workflow reduced workload. The workflow 
extended workload reduction to full text screening and embedded community 
researchers throughout, enabling the completion of a scoping review with nuanced 
eligibility criteria.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Every year, more scientific papers are published. This 
makes it hard for researchers to keep up with all the information when they are 
doing studies that summarize what we know; these studies are called reviews. One 
of the most time-consuming parts of a review is screening thousands of papers 
for fit to the review topic. Researchers usually begin with title and abstract 
screening, which means reading the title and a short summary of each paper 
(called an abstract) to narrow down, before full-text screening, where they read 
entire papers to make final inclusion decisions. Artificial intelligence (AI) 
tools such as machine-learning models can help speed up the review process by 
screening papers. However, many AI tools are developed without knowledge user 
input, which can improve the relevance of review outcomes and uncover nuances in 
the review topic, such as assessing the engagement of lay communities in 
research, which is often inconsistently defined and applied. In this study, we 
implemented an AI-assisted process to support title and abstract and full-text 
screening. We applied the process to a review of approaches used to engage lay 
communities in modeling studies of infectious diseases. The study was led by 
knowledge users from community-based organizations in collaboration with 
academic partners, who together defined the review topic and screened titles and 
abstracts and full texts. First, we trained a machine-learning model on a subset 
of titles and abstracts that were screened by human reviewers. Then, for 
full-text screening, we used a two-step approach: we first narrowed down full 
texts by identifying those that were more likely to fit the review topic based 
on the words and phrases they used, and then applied a second machine-learning 
model trained on full texts screened by human reviewers. The AI-assisted process 
helped us screen more than 9000 papers, reducing screening workload by 48% 
during title and abstract screening and by 81% during full-text screening. These 
findings show that combining AI tools with knowledge user input can support 
reductions in screening workload while accounting for nuanced and inconsistently 
reported information.

Community-acquired Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia in people living with HIV: a

Cillóniz C(1)(2), Campanella A(3), Guglielmi R(3), Malano-Barletta D(4),

OBJECTIVES: To compare the clinical characteristics, management, and outcomes of 
community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) caused by Haemophilus influenzae in people 
living with HIV (PWH) versus HIV-negative patients, and to evaluate whether HIV 
infection independently influences disease severity, intensive care unit (ICU) 
admission, or short- and long-term mortality.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational study of prospectively 
collected data including all consecutive adults hospitalized with CAP at a 
tertiary teaching hospital in Spain between 1996 and 2025. Microbiological 
confirmation of H. influenzae was obtained using standard diagnostic methods. 
Clinical variables, treatments, and outcomes were compared between PWH and 
HIV-negative patients. Propensity score matching (1:3) was applied to adjust for 
baseline differences. Multivariable generalized linear and Cox regression models 
were used to assess the association between HIV status and ICU admission, 
30-day, 90-day, and 1-year mortality.
RESULTS: Among 202 patients, 18 (9%) were PWH. Before matching, PWH were 
younger, more frequently current smokers, and had higher rates of chronic liver 
disease. After propensity score matching, 18 PWH were compared with 54 
HIV-negative controls. No significant differences were observed in disease 
severity, complications, ICU admission, or mortality. No deaths occurred among 
PWH during follow-up. HIV status was not independently associated with ICU 
admission or mortality at any time point. However, confidence intervals were 
wide and the number of events was limited, reducing statistical power and 
precision of estimates.
CONCLUSIONS: In hospitalized patients with H. influenzae CAP, HIV infection was 
not associated with worse short- or long-term outcomes. However, given the small 
sample size and low number of outcome events, clinically meaningful differences 
cannot be excluded. Preventive strategies, including vaccination and optimized 
antiretroviral therapy, remain essential to reduce pneumonia burden in PWH.

Dating Applications as HIV Prevention Ecosystems in the Era of Digital Sexual 
Networks.

(1)Infectious and Tropical Diseases Unit, Department of Medical and Surgical

Dating applications have become central components of contemporary sexual 
networks, yet HIV prevention remains largely organised outside these digital 
environments. We propose that dating applications should be conceptualised as 
potential HIV and sexual health prevention ecosystems, connecting testing, PrEP 
and PEP navigation, STI services, vaccination, telemedicine, partner 
notification, behavioural support, and artificial intelligence-enabled health 
navigation. Existing evidence supports the effectiveness of many of these 
digital interventions individually, while emerging integrated models suggest

improving personalisation and continuity across prevention services. However, 
implementation will require careful attention to privacy, governance, equity, 
healthcare accessibility, and differences across health systems. Rather than 
replacing existing healthcare services, digital prevention ecosystems could 
complement them by bringing prevention closer to the environments where sexual 
interactions increasingly originate.

Ebola Virus Disease in the Era of One Health and Global Preparedness: Evolving 
Epidemiology, Genomic Surveillance, and Future Challenges.

De Maria F(1), Branda F(2), Alexiev I(3), Yon DK(4)(5), Demir AB(6), Ceccarelli 
G(7), Scarpa F(8), Ciccozzi M(2), Russo A(1).

Author information:
(1)Infectious and Tropical Diseases Unit, "Renato Dulbecco" Teaching Hospital of 
Catanzaro, 88100 Catanzaro, Italy.
(2)Unit of Medical Statistics and Molecular Epidemiology, Università Campus 
Bio-Medico di Roma, 00128 Rome, Italy.
(3)National Reference Confirmatory Laboratory of HIV, National Center of 
Infectious and Parasitic Diseases (NCIPD), 1504 Sofia, Bulgaria.
(4)Center for Digital Health, Medical Science Research Institute, Kyung Hee 
University College of Medicine, Seoul 05278, Republic of Korea.
(5)Department of Pediatrics, Kyung Hee University Medical Center, Kyung Hee 
University College of Medicine, Seoul 05278, Republic of Korea.
(6)Department of Medical Biology, Faculty of Medicine, İzmir University of 
Economics, İzmir 35330, Türkiye.
(7)Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases, University Hospital 
Policlinico Umberto I, Sapienza University of Rome, 00185 Rome, Italy.
(8)Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Sassari, 07100 Sassari, 
Italy.

Ebola virus disease (EVD) remains one of the most severe viral hemorrhagic 
fevers, with recurrent outbreaks challenging global healthcare systems. This 
narrative review traces the evolving epidemiology of EVD from the first 
recognized outbreaks in 1976 to the ongoing 2026 Bundibugyo virus public health 
emergency in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. Over nearly 
five decades, the recognized range of Ebola outbreak contexts and amplification 
mechanisms has broadened considerably: rural zoonotic spillovers remain the 
predominant mode of emergence, but the scale and reach of subsequent 
transmission increasingly depend on where introductions occur, on delays in 
detection, on population mobility, on ecological disruption, on armed conflict, 
on healthcare-associated transmission, and on viral persistence in survivors. 
Major advances in molecular epidemiology and genomic surveillance have improved 
outbreak investigation, enabling real-time transmission reconstruction and 
detection of survivor-linked resurgence. Vaccination, particularly ring 
vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV, has shown high effectiveness against Zaire 
ebolavirus, yet vaccine equity gaps and the absence of licensed vaccines for 
Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus remain critical vulnerabilities, though new 
candidate vaccines and therapeutics for Bundibugyo virus entered clinical 
evaluation in mid-2026. Artificial intelligence and digital technologies, 
including AI-assisted early warning systems, portable sequencing, drones, 
blockchain, and mobile health platforms, offer promising tools for outbreak 
preparedness, but robust evidence of their real-world operational impact during 
filovirus outbreaks remains limited, and their deployment in low-resource 
settings faces substantial barriers related to infrastructure, literacy, data 
costs, and governance. Integrated preparedness frameworks that combine 
ecological surveillance, resilient healthcare systems, community engagement, and 
international coordination under a One Health umbrella are increasingly viewed 
as a strategic necessity. The 2026 Bundibugyo outbreak reaffirms that despite 
decades of lessons, structural weaknesses in surveillance, response timeliness, 
and community trust continue to recur. Sustainable, multi-year financing, 
diversified vaccine platforms, regional manufacturing, and local co-design of 
digital tools are essential to translate lessons into lasting change. 
Preparedness is best understood as a continuous process rather than a reactive 
state.

Guideline Concordance of ChatGPT-Generated Responses on Antibiotic Prophylaxis 
in Endodontics.

Diniz FMM(1), Lourenço PR(1), Cruz-Filho AMD(1), Lopes-Olhê FC(1), Mazzi-Chaves 
JF(1), Magri LV(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Restorative Dentistry, School of Dentistry of Ribeirão Preto, 
University of São Paulo (USP), Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo, Brazil.

Antibiotic prophylaxis decision-making in endodontics represents a core 
competency in dental education, requiring the integration of systemic risk 
assessment, guideline interpretation, and antimicrobial stewardship principles. 
Although artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly 
accessed by students and clinicians for clinical guidance, their educational 
reliability in teaching evidence-based antibiotic prophylaxis remains unclear. 
This descriptive study evaluated the accuracy and guideline concordance of 
ChatGPT-5 responses to predefined clinical scenarios in endodontics. Seventeen 
clinically relevant questions grounded in current guidelines from the American 
Heart Association (AHA), American Association of Endodontists (AAE), and 
American Dental Association (ADA) were submitted to the model. Responses were 
independently assessed by an experienced endodontist using a five-point Likert 
scale addressing clinical correctness, guideline concordance, and potential 
educational risk. Quantitative agreement was summarized descriptively, and a 
directed qualitative content analysis examined patterns of correct indication, 
expanded indication, depth of clinical reasoning, and risk of misinterpretation 
from an educational perspective. ChatGPT demonstrated full agreement with 
expert, guideline-based recommendations in 10 of 17 scenarios (58.8%), 
particularly in classical teaching domains such as infective endocarditis 
prophylaxis, antibiotic selection, dosage, and timing. Partial agreement was 
observed in four scenarios (23.5%), primarily due to unnecessary expansion of 
prophylactic indications. Disagreement occurred in three scenarios (17.6%), 
mainly involving immunocompromised conditions, including HIV infection with low 
CD4 counts and chemotherapy-related neutropenia. Although no response was deemed 
clinically unsafe, expanded recommendations in medically complex cases 
represented a potential educational risk for inappropriate antibiotic 
prescribing. The study supports cautious, guideline-based interpretation of 
AI-generated clinical information rather than conclusions about educational 
effectiveness or curricular implementation.

Artificial neuro-fuzzy intelligence for dynamic tracking and prediction of HIV 
prevalence and new infections among individuals aged 15 to 49 years in Uganda: 
Computational national-level models.

Abdalla EAH(1), Elsadig M(2), Omar U(3), Eze VHU(1)(4), Mergani A(5), Salhi 
A(2), Dafalla AM(6), Alkhalig YG(7), Ahmed SM(8), Vahwere BM(9).

Author information:
(1)Department of Electrical, Telecommunication and Computer Engineering, Kampala 
International University, Ishaka, Uganda.
(2)Department of Information Systems, College of Computer and Information 
Sciences, Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
(3)CEO of Kampala International University Teaching Hospital and Research, 
Ishaka, Uganda.
(4)Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Mbarara University of 
Science and Technology, Kihumuro, Uganda.
(5)Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Kampala International 
University, Ishaka, Uganda.
(6)School of Allied Health Sciences, Kampala International University, Ishaka, 
Uganda.
(7)School of Architecture, Computing, and Engineering, University of East 
London, London United Kingdom.
(8)Department of Physiology, Kampala International University, Ishaka, Uganda.
(9)Department of Surgery, Kampala International University, Ishaka, Uganda.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection remains a major global health 
burden, and Uganda continues to experience rising new HIV incidence, making 
prevention and management increasingly challenging. Accurate estimation of HIV 
prevalence (PHIVP) and tracking new HIV incidence (PHIVN) require robust 
computational models to effectively inform public health interventions. This 
study aims to develop a computational tracking model based on a 2-level 
intelligent framework to dynamically monitor PHIVP and PHIVN in Uganda and to 
identify influential factors that contribute to HIV trends among individuals 
aged 15 to 49. Six datasets from 146 Ugandan districts for 2023: sex rate, 
antiretroviral therapy coverage, awareness, education, personal income, and 
historical HIV indicators (prevalence and new incidence) were analyzed. A 
2-level intelligent technique was employed: level I, an upgraded clustering 
algorithm was used to identify optimal parameters influencing PHIVP and PHIVN 
and level II, a neuro-fuzzy model was trained on these parameters to construct 
the computational tracking model. Data were partitioned into 85% for model 
training and 15% for testing and validation. Model accuracy was evaluated using 
regression performance, error metrics, and statistical significance. The model 
predicted a decline in PHIVP from 5.1% to 4.92%, and accurately tracked 37,996 
PHIVN cases out of 38,132 actual incidences. The computational framework 
demonstrated strong predictive performance, yielding high regression values of 
R = 0.832 to 0.987 for PHIVP and PHIVN across 3 scenarios. Statistical analysis 
confirmed model reliability with P < .001 and P = .001. The 2-level intelligent 
approach exhibits strong potential for dynamically monitoring HIV prevalence and 
new incidence in Uganda. The 6 analyzed datasets represent significant 
determinants of PHIVP reduction and PHIVN tracking among adults aged 15 to 49. 
These findings support the feasibility of computational modeling as a tool for 
enhancing HIV surveillance, guiding prevention strategies, and strengthening 
evidence-based public health decision-making in Uganda.

Infectious risks of transfusion: A 10-year look back and perspectives.

Bloch EM(1), Drews SJ(2), Jacobs JW(3).

Author information:
(1)Division of Transfusion Medicine, Department of Pathology, Johns Hopkins 
University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States. Electronic address: 
Ebloch2@jhmi.edu.
(2)Surveillance and Discovery Laboratory, Canadian Blood Services, Ottawa, 
Ontario, Canada; Medical Microbiology, Canadian Blood Services, Edmonton, 
Alberta, Canada; Division of Diagnostic and Applied Microbiology, Department of 
Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, & Women and Children's Health Research 
Institute, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada.
(3)Department of Pathology, Microbiology and Immunology, Vanderbilt University, 
Nashville, TN, United States.

Almost 50 years following the advent -and ensuing tragedy- of 
transfusion-transmitted HIV, infectious diseases continue to shape blood 
transfusion practice and policy. Over the past decade alone, a myriad of changes 
span innovation in donor selection, testing and pathogen reduction, to emergence 
and re-emergence pathogens that have required evaluation and, in some cases, 
active intervention. Major developments include refined bacterial testing, novel 
findings on cold storage of platelets along with the expanded use of pathogen 
reduction to address the risk of bacterial contamination. Notable pathogens 
include Zika virus, Plasmodium (malaria), Babesia (babesiosis) and SARS-CoV-2 
(COVID-19), the latter spurring a historic pandemic. SARS-CoV-2 highlighted the 
potential for emerging infectious diseases to impact the blood supply, 
independent of whether transfusion transmissible. The pandemic afforded new 
insight into convalescent plasma and how passive immunotherapy can be used to 
treat infectious diseases. Other favorable developments include a transition to 
individualized risk assessment and the relaxation of longstanding donor deferral 
policies (e.g. variant Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease), which have helped to 
alleviate the transfusion deficit. Progress in artificial intelligence and 
machine learning has yielded novel tools for surveillance and horizon scanning 
that enable early recognition of threats and opportunities for transfusion 
services to contend with infectious diseases. Nonetheless, many of the favorable 
developments do not extend to low and low-middle income countries, where 
replacement donation, suboptimal laboratory-based screening with limited 
molecular testing, and near-absent post-transfusion surveillance, continue to 
contribute to transfusion-transmitted infection. We reflect on the impact of 
infectious diseases on transfusion services over the last ten years (2016-2026).
